newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: LGT details profits, strategic outlook.
newsitem.headline: LGT details profits, strategic outlook.

text.p: Liechtenstein Global Trust, with over 100 billion Swiss francs ($67.5 billion) under management and advisement, said a 35 percent rise in its group earnings in 1996 was due largely to favourable currency exchange rates and gains in world securities markets.

Consolidated group profit rose 35 percent, or by 45.3 million Swiss francs, to 174.1 million francs in 1996, from 128.9 million in 1995. The group also plans to raise its dividend to 22 francs from 20 francs.

It is targeting a return on equity of 18 to 20 percent in future, compared with 14.7 percent for 1996, based on the profit of 174 million francs and shareholders' funds of 1.183 billion francs. In 1995 the ROE was 11.9 percent.
At a news briefing, Prince Philipp von und zu Liechtenstein, chairman and chief executive officer, said developments were "especially positive in the second half".

Profits were not substantially affected by the acquisition of U.S. institutional fund manager Chancellor Capital Management Inc, LGT said. The purchase was completed in October. The goodwill charge of 309 million from the transaction will be amortised over twenty years.

The goodwill charge for Chancellor amounted to 2.3 million francs in 1996. LGT also said it has adopted International Accounting Standards, which led to some minor revisions to its stated 1995 results.
With the acquisition of Chancellor, assets under administration at the end of 1996 totalled 114.5 billion Swiss francs, compared with 52.9 billion at the end of 1995.

LGT opened a bank in Vienna early this year, and did not rule out acquisitions in the European private banking sector in future. With respect to its plans for possible acquisitions, Prince Philipp said such a move in Germany or elsewhere in Europe would "certainly be possible," but any such acquisition would have to be a good match for LGT's own culture and strategy.
In February, LGT said it had appointed Anton Schwaiger to a new post of chief operating officer.

Schwaiger, previously responsible for private banking in the group will also take over duties of David Minella, former president of LGT's asset management division, after Minella decided to resign, LGT executives said.

With respect to the changes in management, finance director Rolf Wickenkamp, who has been named to LGT's three-member executive management group, said that the changes would "strengthen the top management."
Prince Philipp said the move would likely produce synergies between the asset management and private banking divisions.
Schwaiger emphasised that the move did not reflect a change in strategy to shift more emphasis to private banking.

LGT said it was pleased with launch of Castle Alternative Invest AG last September, a fund investing hedge funds, which is now fully invested at about 190 million francs. LGT is launching a second product called Castle Private Equity.
Private equity funds give investors indirect access to venture capital, development capital, management buyouts and other similar investments.
Demand for such funds has been strong in the U.S. and the U.K., especially from institutional investors.
But changes are also taking place in Europe as more small companies begin to seek bourse listings. This is likely to make such funds popular elsewhere in Europe.
"I think the private equity boom will is now coming to Europe," said Schwaiger.
